doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: Is jazz America's only art form
summary: They discuss the African-American roots of blues, rock and jazz and the art-versus-popular distinction.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I’ve seen many times the phrase jazz is America’s only original art form. And I sort of agree but then I think well what about the blues, and if we’re calling rock & roll art now, I guess what I’m trying to say is it’s wonderful that so many forms of music started here and then got spread around the world.

Yeah. Terms are tossed around quite loosely. “Artist” — there’s a loose definition to that. And the African-American experience is so unto its own. You know this experience, in this country, created everything you’re talking about: blues, rock & roll, jazz, it’s all part of the same experience. But I know what you mean, they make the distinction that jazz is an art form, the only true American art form because blues and rock & roll and the other things were thought of as popular music and jazz is thought of more as an art music.
But jazz was popular music when it started.

And the categories, and rock & roll has broken all the boundaries and definitions and borders as well. I mean have you heard — there’s so many sub-genres in rock & roll, and there’s some incredible things that have happened. I don’t know a jazz musician that doesn’t respect the work of Zappa you know. I love Bjork. Now what is that music? You know? But yeah, jazz as an art form — I mean I hear all the time too, I don’t know how true that is, I don’t know how you define art, but I hear that quite a bit.
